title: Roguelike Roundup 10/24 - 11/7
content:
In the Roguelike Roundup, Jake sifts through the deluge of roguelikes and autobattlers that come out every couple of weeks to shout out the ones he thinks are worth your time.

Outcast Tales

Even before I started the game up, I had one thought: What’s the catch? You see, the game is free. No, not free (we have designed the game to make you buy microtransactions). Not free (it’s time-gated unless you pay more). Just straight up zero dollars and zero cents. In fact, the devs actively don’t want you to even give them money.

Initially, I assumed this was some sort of marketing stunt or weird AI scam, but the publisher of the game–Inner Pocket–published Burn With Me, which I covered previously. So that’s legit, and the game is legit, so…what’s the catch?

There isn’t one. Hardlane Studio accomplished the monumental task of bringing a game into being and gave it to the world for free because they want people to enjoy the art they made. As the unfortunate victim of multiple layoffs in the game industry, I find this deeply moving. The entire industry has, for a long time, operated via the exploitation of people wanting desperately to make art. To see a group of people go against that trend, to look the slavering juggernaut that is the games industry and capitalism at large in the eyes and say no. That’s beautiful. They said the best way to support them is to get word out about the game, so that is what I’m doing.

Outcast Tales is a party-based tactical roguelike whose story plays out through random events and skill checks. The writing is fun and campy, reminiscent of early Fallout. Each party member will have a personality, which can be chosen or randomly generated at the start of each run. This personality will alter how they gain morale through events and how the world reacts to them. The veteran personality will have bandits reacting in fear, whereas the prophet may partake of the potentially toxic mushroom whether you like it or not.

Gameplay-wise, Outcast Tales doesn’t break the mold but has a solid flow to it. Each ability is exhausted upon use, and you can use them again once you use their core ability. Most characters have some way of giving Ability Boost, which dramatically increases the scaling of your next ability. When you finish a fight, one character levels up and a randomly chosen ability can be upgraded in several ways or replaced by a different one outright. I was pretty impressed by the diversity of builds from the several hours I spent playing.

Overall, Outcast Tales is not going to blow you away in terms of gameplay, but the writing and, well, freeness should compel you to try it out. At the very least it has several hours of content and a unique world to sink your teeth into.

Worship

Have you ever played Pikmin and thought, “I wish I could be a more active force in the death of my Pikmin?” Then boy do I have a game for you. Worship from Chasing Rats Games has had my eye ever since its debut trailer and has finally launched. A twisted take on Pikmin where you lead a cult devoted to a dark god of your choosing to destroy the world.

Okay, I know I’ve said Pikmin three times already (four now), but that’s not really what this game is about. The real main mechanic is casting spells via drawing runes on the ground in someone’s blood. It can be yours or one of your followers, the gods aren’t picky. Bleed a circle around a group of nonbelievers to ‘recruit’ them. Bleed a square to empower yourself to throw ghastly hands at your enemies. There are many more shapes and combinations to discover that do even more interesting things, but I’ll leave that for you to discover.

Speaking of discovery, the game has a lot for you to stumble upon. In your quest to grow your influence and challenge the champions of good, you’ll come across many different puzzles/quests. Reassemble a band of cursed, skeletal musicians and bring a haunted town to life; unchain a dark god; spill your minion’s blood to inspire a painter. These are just a few of the scenarios I found on my first few runs.

The world itself is shockingly vibrant for being primarily in black and white. The small splashes of color that usually represent the various enemy factions immediately pop, as does the blood you spill. The music ranges from crunchy guitar riffs to banjos and all of it is great. A special standout are the eldritch gods themselves. Not only do they have really unique aesthetic designs, but their lore is really compelling. It's genuinely difficult to create dark patrons that aren’t derivative, and the unique flavor of each of the ones I’ve unlocked so far have me jonesing for more.

As a certified hater of the Survival game and Base Building genre of games, I was initially concerned with the idea of growing a cult in an open map. I’m very happy to report there is no tedious resource collection or building required. Each run takes you through three maps, separated by boss fights, and while your cultist compound is present in each as a place to drop off eldritch goodies and unlock relics, that’s where it ends. The main thing that turned me off of similar games like Cult of the Lamb was that it was clearly focused on the cult part, with combat and frenetic gameplay as a secondary concern. In Worship, not only is combat a significant chunk of the game, but it’s good. Siccing minions on enemies and drawing glyphs to empower and recharge your spells all while dodging attacks is engaging and fun as hell. The boss fights specifically felt really unique and impactful.

I like my games with a good bit of challenge, so I am a bit disappointed to say that Worship is quite easy. I have completed three runs so far without losing or even coming particularly close, and whether or not that’s bad is for you to judge.  Overall though, I strongly endorse this game. It's oozing with charm and has a really unique and compelling gameplay loop.

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 46: Ettin RTT Prep
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I was plugging along with more hobby progress on my Red Corsairs, and slowly coming to terms with the idea that I'm going to have to run them at Worlds. This time around I'm mostly doing hobby work and running HeroQuest with the kids, plus I'm prepping for an RTT this weekend.

Hobby Progress

I'm still working on the Red Corsairs. Right now the goal is to add Valthex and Mutilators by the Grand Narrative, plus finish the Chosen if I can get that far. I'm making good time on the Mutilators, which despite being complex models are fun to paint and may be done by Saturday. I finished the first one last night:

I'm really happy with how this guy turned out - I think he looks great and I'm a big fan of how saturated the new Tone Pro reds look, though it does make him look markedly brighter than my existing Red Corsairs - I'm going to have to match the next batch of Terminators to the existing ones. I've started working on the other two, and I'm hoping to finish them faster now that I have a good idea of how I want the scheme on these to go.

The drills from the Assault Centurions just ended up being perfect on these and I'm so happy with the results. It was absolutely worth tracking those down and ordering a set so I could use the bits.

Prep for the Ettin RTT

I haven't been playing nearly enough games, and I'm getting rusty. I need to get some games in before the Grand Narrative, and as luck would have it, there's a 3-round RTT coming up this weekend at a local game shop. I went ahead and signed up for it, and my plan is to take the Red Corsairs, get in three relatively easy games, probably go 2-1, and win best painted. It's more about a refresher than anything else and I'm not planning to bring anything overly competitive at this point. I desperately need those mutilators and at least five more terminators and another Terminator Sorcerer to make this work, and that's not all getting painted by Saturday. Could be doable by the Grand Narrative, however. I need to work on this and get it all ready soon, and plan on using Thanksgiving break as my key painting time for the World Championships.

The weird piece here is the Master of Executions running Touched by the Warp - he gives Huron's unit PSYCHIC, and that's basically just to make their ranged attacks better. That's not very good, but it might be enough for some fun turnarounds here. The other value of running Veterans of the Long War here is getting full re-rolls to hit and having two very good reactive moves, so I can at least pull off some bullshit when I need to.

My general plan is to try and stall the board early and control the middle with that unit of Fabius + Chosen + the Masters, which is conveniently a PSYKER unit with T6 and the ability to shrug off some damage. We'll see how it pans out.

Final Thoughts

That does it for this week - I'm all in now on painting as prep for this weekend and while I don't expect to win three games, it'll be good practice and I'll at least have a good shot at best painted with this particular army. They look really good, and I'm happy with how the reds are turning out. I need to do a bit more work on the Legionaries and get them to a level I'm happy with but right now there's a lot to like.

See you next Thursday.

title: Upland & Prairie is a tame board game with a wild theme
content:
Our Verdict

The hex map and tokens may give the impression this is a crunchy game, but it isn't. The hopeful environmental theme is a good match for lightweight tactical gameplay - something to play on the couch when you just need to unwind.

Pros
  • Lovely art
  • Relaxing, low conflict gameplay
Cons
  • All tactics, no strategy

Designed by Peer Sylvester, Upland & Prairie is a lightweight and very attractive little board game of returning wildlife to the Scottish uplands or the Montana prairie. It offers a quick to play tactical puzzle that's fun, relaxing, but far from revolutionary.

I asked for a review sample of Upland & Prairie from publisher Osprey - and as part of Wargamer's constant search for worthy titles for our guide to the best board games, of course. In a past career in the zoo industry my partner kept lynx, and she's worked on native species reintroduction projects; I was interested to learn if the game's mechanics engage with any of the complexities of apex species reintroductions.

Reader, it does not. Upland & Prairie isn't a deep investigation of human-animal conflict or environmental restoration. The environmental theme carries through the art and components, illustrated by scientific illustrator Hannah Cohen, and they creep into the mechanics here and there - there are also some good suggestions for further reading at the back of the rulebook. But this game is too slight to have a huge amount to say on the topic.

Play begins by creating a hexmap of either the Scottish uplands or Montanan prairie using reversible tiles. Each turn you'll draw three animal tokens from a shared bag. These come in three different types, with double-sided art to reflect the two different landscapes the game takes place in: you've got a lynx or mountain lion, a tawny owl or burrowing owl, and a pine marten or black-footed ferret.

You return one animal, place one behind your screen for end-game scoring, and one goes out anywhere on the map. Initially, hexes can only contain one animal, but a progression system - slightly different for each biome - allows more animals to co-exist as the game goes on. In practical terms this allows animals to create routes through one another's territory (double-down in one area to block others out), but it also nicely reflects how that biodiversity enables biodensity.

You're working towards two possible end-game conditions. If the players completely rewild the environment and emptying the token bag, then whoever has the most complete sets of all three animals wins.

But the map tiles also contain special goal locations which match up with those on other tiles - paired goals which you'll place far apart, and slightly closer triple goals - and if one animal species makes an unbroken path that connects the locations in either set, then whichever player has the most of that animal behind their screen wins.

The fact you don't "own" any of the animals that are on the board may be intended to show the hands-off approach of animal reintroductions. But the fact you have an investment in them which you can change during the game creates a parallel with an unexpected game genre: Upland & Prairie is a diminutive, lightweight relative of the epic railway building 18XX genre, in the same way that the rodent-like rock hyrax is the closest evolutionary relative of the elephant.

This gameplay is light. Victory comes from identifying which animal is closer to completing a winning route, and making an educated guess about which player has a bigger investment in it. If you think you're ahead of your opponent on the leading animal, you can push towards a victory with it; if you're unsure, you need to block it from winning.

It's purely tactical, not strategic. That's not a bad thing, but it's not what you generally associate with hexes, counters, and painting the map red. I've found all my games of Upland & Prairie to be interesting and fun, but neither antagonistic nor particularly challenging. It's a chill-out game, the board game equivalent of flicking on the TV or booting up a comfort videogame. There's a place for those.

title: Rare 'grail' Warhammer board game returns, but without its iconic Old World theme
content:
Restoration Games, known for remastering out-of-print 'holy grail' board games, has revealed a new licensing deal with Games Workshop. That means three vintage Warhammer board games are making a comeback! However, they've had quite a significant makeover.

The one game that has the internet most excited is Chaos in the Old World. Designed by the esteemed Eric Lang (Blood Rage, Cthulhu: Death May Die) in 2009, this asymmetric area control game was loved for its blend of storytelling and strategy.

I've not played it myself, but our in-house Warhammer 40k expert Tim Linward tells me the game was "fucking mint". Lang himself says in a Restoration Games press release: "I think Chaos in the Old World is my most requested reprint from the most dedicated fans".

It was a unique asymmetric game, with interesting decks designed around the modus operandi of the Chaos gods you played. The Old World theme did serious heavy lifting for some fans - and for them, I have bad news.

Devastation in the Dread World, as it's now called, is no longer set in Warhammer's Old World. All mention of Chaos Gods and their servants seems to have been stripped. Instead, a Restoration Games says it takes place in the 'Talisman Realm'. "Games Workshop's new, expanded brand" is a multiverse-style setting that covers worlds outside the Warhammer universe.

Restoration Games explains on Reddit that this multiverse includes the worlds of board games like Talisman and Fury of Dracula, as well as Gravemarch, the original setting of Devastation in the Dread World. Gravemarch is "a place of high fantasy, teeming with malevolent factions, vying for control over the few pockets of humanity that remain".

It's also the setting for the other remasters announced. While Devastation in the Dread World heads to crowdfunding early next year, Restoration Games plans to release Dungeons of Gravemarch: The Card Game and Warrior Knights in 2028. The first is a restoration of 2010's Space Hulk: Death Angel - The Card Game, designed by Corey Konieczka (Battlestar Galactica, Star Wars: Rebellion, Mansions of Madness). The latter is a remaster of the 1985 title of the same name.

If you're not familiar with Restoration Games, there's a reason I'm calling these games 'restorations', not 'reprints'. Restoration Games brings loved games from decades past into the hobby's modern era, and that often means updating the gameplay.

As the publisher says in a Reddit comment: "There are definitely some revisions of the gameplay" in Devastation in the Dread World, "things Eric has been noodling on for over a decade". "For example, we've got some new factions that do some cool things, and we've got some more scenario-based play as opposed to the rather random event deck system."

"We're stoked to be working with Games Workshop as a partner in general and to help them build out the whole concept of the Talisman Realm in particular", the publisher adds in another comment. "They have some cool stuff planned. This is just the first wave of stuff. There are other worlds and other games in the pipeline as well."

Want even more Warhammer? We can recommend some digital Warhammer 40k games in our linked guide. Or, you can head to our official Wargamer Discord for a chat with fellow fans.

title: D&D revives 3.5e viking sheep-taur species after 22 years
content:
D&D is bringing back support for a species that hasn't been officially playable for 22 years in the November D&D Beyond drop. The Bariaur is a centaur-esque D&D race with the torso of a human, the body of a sheep or goat, and ram horns.

Last playable in 3.5e's Planar Handbook, this is a celestial 'planar race' typically associated with the Planescape setting. It specifically lives in the Norse-inspired Ysgard, an upper plane of giants and viking warriors, fighting for good.

Now we have 5.5's version of the species, which gives Bariaur's proficiency in some outdoorsy skills, and a resistance to (advantage against) being knocked prone - thanks to those extra legs. They also get a special ram attack, where - after moving at least 10 feet towards an enemy - they can use both the damage and shove options for an unarmed attack. Perhaps they'd make a good monk?

Oh, and of course, they get Darkvision too - even though I'm pretty sure that's not an ability they had in the past, it's basically the default now. Sheep can see surprisingly well in the dark, so I guess it fits?

The new D&D drop is focused on Ysgard and, along with the Bariaur, contains new monsters like the Valkyrie and Dread Linnorm, new maps including one around the World Tree's roots, new feats, and new weapons like the bola and the pitchfork.

While we haven't had the option to play as a (non-homebrew) Bariaur, it's not true to say the sheeptaurs have been totally absent for the last two decades. In fact, they were around in 2023's mixed bag Planescape revival, appearing both in Morte's Planar Parade and the adventure Turn of Fortune's Wheel.

Are you going to be rolling up a Bariaur in your next campaign? What other types of -taur should Wizards make? Let us know on the Wargamer Discord.

title: How to Paint Everything: Marvel Crisis Protocol - Iron Lad
content:
Hey everybody, I'm back with another How to Paint Everything: Marvel Crisis Protocol and this time we are looking for the time-displaced younger version of Kang the Conqueror, Iron Lad! This model can be found in the Iron Lad, Iron Monger, Kang the Conqueror & Rescue Character Pack.

Like many of the "Iron-Suit" characters, Iron Lad's model features a cool blast off effect and this time it features a ring of clouds surrounding the rocket boot blasts. This give a very neat effect that he's punching through the air while flying.

For Iron Lad's paint job, we are going to look at painting non-metallic metal red and silver as well as fire and cloud effects. As always, you can find the colors that were used on this paint job in a handy-dandy paint chart below.

Let's get to it and paint up Iron Lad!

Credit - Brushwizard

Red Armor

Basecoat - Citadel Rhinox Hide

Layer - Citadel Rhinox Hide: Army Painter Dragon Red

Layer - Army Painter Dragon Red

Highlight - Army Painter Angelic Red

Highlight - Army Painter Flickering Flame

Highlight - AK Interactive White

Non-metallic red is one of my favorite things to paint, and the key to it is a nice, solid basecoat of Rhinox Hide. It's such a great color and over the years, it's become a staple for many other color recipes as well. The next step is to mix Rhinox Hide with Dragon Red and paint this onto any areas that will be catching light, while leaving the Rhinox Hide showing. This will enforce contrast later. Next, we paint Dragon Red on top of the previous layer, also leaving the Red and Brown mix showing.

Highlights are started with Angelic Red on top of the previous layer and on all of the sharp edges. This is followed by another edge highlight with Flickering Flame, and finally, another, more controlled highlight of White.

Silver Armor

Basecoat - AK Interactive French Blue

Shadows - AK Interactive Dark Sea Blue

Layer - AK Interactive French Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive Snow Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive White

Dark Lining - AK Interactive Black

Iron Lad's silver armor sections started with a basecoat of French Blue; the shadows and recesses were then painted Dark Sea Blue. This was followed by a clean-up layer of French Blue. Highlights started with a layer of Snow Blue over the French Blue areas and on any edges, followed by another highlight of White. To enforce the contrast, we line the armor panels and recesses with Black.

Repulsor and Eye Glow

Basecoat - AK Interactive White

Layer - Lethal Shadows Fluorescent Light Orange

All of the glowing sections of the armor were given a basecoat of White and a layer of Fluorescent Light Orange.

Blast Effect

Basecoat - Army Painter Warp Yellow

Layer - Army Painter Flickering Flame

Layer - Army Painter Angelic Red

Highlight - Army Painter Aegis Aqua

Highlight - AK Interactive White

The main lower section of the blast-off effect was painted Warp Yellow. Once it was dry, I added a layer of Flickering Flame to it and added a bit of Warp Yellow onto the surface as well, to wet-blend the two colors together. This was followed by a layer of Angelic Red, which was wet-blended into Flickering Flame.

The upper section also started with a layer of Warp Yellow, which was blended into Aegis Aqua near the top of the column of fire. The blast effect under his boot started with Aegis Aqua and was highlighted with White to finish it off.

Cloud Effects

Basecoat - Army Painter Ash Grey

Layer - Army Painter Brigade Grey

Layer - AK Interactive White

The ring of clouds around his blast effect started with a layer of Ash Grey. I then used Brigade Grey and painted globs of grey around the surface of the cloud rings to simulate the shape of the cloud. This was also done with White, overlapping the previous layers.

Concrete Basing

Basecoat - Citadel Stormvermin Fur

Stipple - Army Painter Ash Grey

Stipple - Army Painter Brigade Grey

Wash - Citadel Nuln Oil

As usual, my main go-to for painting concrete basing is to start with a layer of Stormvermin Fur. The surface is then stippled with Ash Grey and Brigade Grey to add a bit of texture to the surface. It's then finished off with a wash of Nuln Oil to get some shadows into the recesses and tie the colors together.

Credit - Brushwizard

Will young Nate break away from the threads of fate and keep himself from becoming Kang the Conqueror? Or is he destined to always return to the mantle of Kang? title: [40k] Tabletop Battles Hot Take: Rules Updates for the 2026 World Championships of Warhammer
content:
Games Workshop published a new site today for their Warhammer Events, and with it, the long-awaited rules updates for Warhammer 40,000 ahead of the 2026 World Championships. This rules update, intended for use at the 2026 World Championships, act as a sort of “stopgap” between the September Balance update and the next, outlining a number of rulings and common rules problems ahead of the event, giving players some much-needed guidance on a few things.

In this article, we’ll be covering the changes, what they mean, and just as importantly - what they missed.

Core Rules Updates

Most of the rulings and updates here concern characters, specifically characters attached to units, though there are a few things here about terrain and movement.

Attached Characters

  • Revived characters which come back as a new unit lose their ‘while leading abilities’ benefits
  • If an attached character’s BODYGUARD unit had an enhancement and is destroyed, the character loses the benefit of the enhancement
  • If you split a unit with an attached character into multiple units, only the part of the unit which retains the attached character benefits from the leader’s benefits
  • If you gave an upgrade enhancement to a CHARACTER leader/support unit and attached it to another unit, when your attached character is destroyed, the attached unit loses the effects of the leader’s upgrade enhancement.

Desperate Escape Tests and Units Which Can Move Through Models 

If you fall back with a unit that can move through all types of model, you don’t have to activate Desperate Escape mode when making your Fall Back move. Makes sense, but this serves as a good catchall for abilities that work like fly but aren’t, such as Necrons phasing through walls.

Fighting on Death: Act Like You Have 1 Wound Left

This clears up questions around bracketing on vehicles and other big units.

INFANTRY/BEASTS/SWARM models don’t move vertically when going over dense terrain features that are less than 2” in height.

Not sure I’d ever seen this come up but sure.

Units selected to shoot but which make no attacks remain hidden.

This is a fun quirk, in that you can select a unit to shoot to get some benefit, then opt to make no attacks, and not lose your hidden status. This also applies if you are selected to shoot, but for some reason don't get to (e.g. your opponent activates a Stratagem that stops a unit being targeted. Good for the shoot-and-scoot crowd. Edit: Not quite - our Discord has points out that rule 04.03.04 specifically says that to qualify as having "shot" a unit needs to make at least one attack. Since most shoot-and-scoots happen after a unit has shot, if you make no attacks you won't get to do them. Some of the other things below such as opportunistically deciding not to shoot as AdMech do still work!

TheChirurgeon: This one caused a powerful stir in our competitive discussion channel, because the question of “can you activate a unit to shoot and make zero attacks?” is a touch controversial. As written we believe this to be the case, given the sequence for ranged attacks has you nominate a unit to shoot, then for each model in the unit you can pick one or more ranged weapons that model has to make attacks, giving you the option of picking zero. This also matters for the Adeptus Mechanicus, where the Baffling Data Screed ability on Tech-Priests lets them roll a D6 when their unit is selected and on a 2+, they can stay hidden after shooting. With this particular ruling you can now select them to shoot, roll, and if they fail the role, opt to shoot no weapons and stay hidden, risking nothing.

This also has big implications for the Phobos Strike Force, where the detachment rule lets you choose to stay hidden or move D6” after shooting - now you can opt to shoot and make no attacks, staying hidden and also moving D6”. 

Stratagems with Multiple Targets

You can’t use a Stratagem which requires a stated number of units if you don’t have that many eligible units, i.e. if you need to target two friendly units and you only have one, you’re out of luck.

Devastating Wounds and Damage Modifiers

They’ve added an FAQ stating that abilities that reduce damage work against [DEVASTATING WOUNDS]. One would hope that this comes with an actual rules addendum in the formal update, as it is currently just a “because we said so” FAQ rather than an actual rules entry. Previously whether these abilities worked on Devastating Wounds depended entirely on the specific wording of the effect.

Strategic Reserves and Ingress Moves

  • If you have an ability which allows a unit to to treat the battle round number as one higher than it is for a unit in Strategic Reserves, you can use it to make an ingress move in your first turn.
  • If a unit goes back into Strategic Reserves with an ability that says it has to make an ingress move in the/your next Movement phase, it can do so on the first turn.

These were both pretty clear and used in tenth but somewhere along the way in the transition to 11th wording changed and we needed new clarification for them.

Surge Moves don’t have to go the full distance, apparently.

A model making a surge move doesn’t have to move the maximum distance permitted by the move. What are we even doing here?

Mission Updates

There are four FAQs covered here, three of them relating to Lions of the Emperor and the Unleash the Lions stratagem. The first two cover the unit splitting and persisting effects - for both the Consecration primary mission as well as the Beacon secondary mission they are no longer eligible units for scoring. The third Lions interaction is that if the unit being targeted is condemned, then it does count as leaving the battlefield. All reasonable answers here, nothing too surprising - but good to see clear answers on these.

The last entry is a bit of a head-scratcher - it states that if you are being set up within 6” of the battlefield edge and there is a terrain feature at 6” from the battlefield edge you can perform actions on this terrain feature (e.g. Plunder) or contest it if the terrain feature is an objective.

TheChirurgeon: I don’t understand this at all. If the visible distance between a terrain feature and the edge of the table is 6”, then isn’t it implied that the terrain feature is more than 6” from the edge of the battlefield? How does deploying within 6” put you on the terrain? This suggests that a terrain feature 6” away from the battlefield edge is now considered to be within 6” of the battlefield edge, which OK makes some kind of sense but has really bad implications for terrain features that are on the line of your deployment zone - they’re now “in’ your deployment zone. Thankfully I don’t think this puts any new terrain features/objectives into deployment zones on the current layouts, but that feels more like a bullet dodged.

Faction Updates

Most of these updates cover outstanding FAQs, with some small tweaks to profiles for Space Marines and Chaos Space Marines.

Adepta Sororitas: You can use Miracle Dice Generated from a Character’s Death when they stand back up with Divine Intervention

This resolves an interesting timing question around when those dice are generated and used for the purposes of standing up with more wounds.

Adeptus Custodes: Shield-Captains can use their Master of of Ka’tahs ability to activate both the Dacatarai and Kaptaris abilities in the same phase

Jag the Power Armor Enthusiast: Custodes Shield Captains can in fact activate their stance re-up in the same phase! While this was assumed, the confirmation is very welcomed and makes shield captains even better than they already were.

Unleash the Lions

There were a number of rulings and changes here to a very complicated Stratagem:

  • Using this Stratagem does not count as destroying the unit.
  • The unit does count as having left the battlefield.
  • Using the Stratagem does not spread persisting effects to the split-off models.
  • Using the Stratagem does reload once per Battle Abilities on the split units.
  • Splitting a unit effectively breaks focused abilities like the Blade Champion's +1 to wound as the unit no longer exists but wasn’t destroyed, and a new unit cannot be targeted.

Jag the Power Armor Enthusiast: Lions of The Emperor… GW, Jesus, you had to say this much? To Summate: No, using Lions doesn't count as destroying them; they do count as leaving the battlefield; no, persisting effects do NOT stay on all the models once you use Unleash the Lions. (Failgrim catches another nerf indirectly from this, for the love of Slaanesh GW why do you hate him so much?!) You also now reload an Allarus Captain's once Per Battle abilities if he's part of the Unit that splits off! This is a very good buff for Allarus Shield Captains. Because here, let me teleport him over to push a button or hold an objective late game! Or reload a stance if you used it last round, for just the SC, Dread Host stonks go UP with this little note! We’re still not done! Here, want to make AdMech players and anyone with a targeted +1 to wound or similar ability in general lose the last bit of hope they didn’t even know they still had? Just wait for them to target the unit, and then use unleash the Lions next turn and break it! This certainly won't be a bad idea and cause feels bad moments, nope, not at all!

Aeldari: Dragon Knights can use multiple Dracolithe tokens against the same unit that ended a move within 8”.

Stunt on those hoes.

Astra Militarum: When using Summary Execution or Brutal Disciplinarian to remove battle-shock, you don’t regain the effects of issued orders.

Those soldiers apparently forgot what you were talking about earlier. They’re cool now, though.

Astra Militarum: A battle-shocked Kasrkin unit can use its Warrior Elite ability to pick an order.

This apparently doesn’t count as issuing an order, and you don’t “become” battle-shocked. So they can have an order applied to them, as a treat. You can’t improve your OC with this - it becomes ‘-’ when Battle-shocked - but you can use it to get Take Aim on your last two meltagunners, which is nice.

Blood Angels: Weapons and Base Tweaks

Mephiston’s Plasma Pistol ganed [HAZARDOUS], the plasma pistol on Death Company Captains gained [CLOSE QUARTERS], and the Twin Heavy Bolter on the Death Company Dreadnought has [RAPID FIRE 2]. They did not fix the thunder hammer on the Blood Angels Captain lacking Dev Wounds. Dante is on a 50mm base now in the Tournament Companion.

Chaos Daemons: Pink Horrors can still split if the attached CHARACTER survives.

You’ll have to kill absolutely everything in one activation if you want to avoid splitting.

Chaos Space Marines: Weapon Tweaks

Chaos Bikers get S5 AP-1 combi-bolters and Nemesis Claw get S5 close combat weapons. Sure, now make Bikers 4W like Outriders.

The Deathwatch Terminators Thing

Deathwatch Terminators saw one major change - their plasma cannon was reduced from Strength 9/10 to 7/8, bringing them in line with the plasma cannon wielded by the Deathwing Terminator Squad. They also added a caveat to Dark Angels army rule entry stating that Deathwatch Terminator Squad units do not gain the DEATHWING keyword despite being Terminator units.

Curie: This was needed; for anyone not aware you could run Deathwatch Terminators using the Deathwatch Support detachment and they’d benefit from the Inner Circle Task Force detachment as well, giving them +1 to wound against units on the vowed objective marker. It gave them access to an additional fight on death stratagem, as well as a stratagem for setting up from Deep Strike outside of 6” instead of 8”. As sad as this makes me as someone who was running the army and abusing this interaction, it’s for the better.

Jag the Power Armor Enthusiast: I really don't know if I agree with the decision to punish Deathwatch players’ units for this. Yes it's a needed nerf, but there were better ways to nerf this, especially as this doesn't solve the other major combo of Ultramarines taking DW Terms and using Guilliman and the Terminator Detachment to supercharge two squads. The easier solution would have been to say that Deathwatch Terms do not benefit from other Chapter abilities, so that way the UM/DW Castle of Death doesn't instantly delete armies. Or, hike the points on Plasma Cannons or limit them to one per 5, which would cut down on this problem immediately.

TheChirurgeon: None of these people are “Deathwatch Players,” only people running “Deathwatch Terminators,” and I’ll bet all the money in my pockets that when they do they’re typically painted as some other chapter. But yeah, generally the Deathwatch Terminator situation sucks and the Deathwatch Support Detachment needs to be violently uprooted from the game.

Jag: You are of course right, this is meta chasers abusing what was likely meant as a fluffy detachment but now anyone who wants to play Deathwatch itself catching a stray because of the Competitive Crowd abusing GW's oddball writing choices with Deathwatch on the whole. There are better ways to fix this in my opinion.

TheChirurgeon: I am once again banging a drum labeled “LEGENDS DETACHMENTS” to cover stuff that looks cool and lets armies mix in ways that can break the game.

Jag: Or, you know, add a specific thing, like a mode for narrative play that is long-form, and has consequences and rewards for fluff centric play. It could even have special rules for each army… oh well, such a thing is probably too complex for a small company like Games Workshop.

Death Guard: Shambling Wall Nerfed/Fixed

A set of changes to Shambling Wall make it work as intended in 11th edition, so now you no longer get to roll saves prior to picking up your Poxwalkers. Also note that Devastating Wounds from critical wounds fall outside of this sequence and so can’t be in the pool of wounds that go to your Poxwalkers when you absorb attacks via the Stratagem.

Drukhari: The Double-cross Stratagem

All of these rulings are about the Double-cross Stratagem from the Kabalite Cartel Detachment. This is another ability where you’re passing wounds off to another unit, and now this has been updated to reflect 11th edition sequencing, having your opponent pick a wound in their pool, end the attack sequence, and do mortal wounds equal to the attack’s D characteristic. They then repeat these steps until there are none left. Devastating Wounds don’t add to this pool and can’t be absorbed, and you get to roll your Feel No Pain rolls.

Imperial Agents: Detachment Tweaks

You can theoretically pick Detachments from outside the book now.

Imperial Knights: Sir Hekhtur and Oaths

Canis Rex no longer counts as having left the battlefield until Hekhtur is destroyed, so it won’t trigger key effects like being Condemned. When you make your Lay Low the Tyrant oath as an additional oath for Heroes of Legend, that’s also when you pick the character in your opponent’s army.

Iron Hands: Their Detachments can’t have other Chapters.

A tweak they made across the board here on some Chapter Detachments which were clearly missing some intended wording and allowing for a lot of potential misuse.

Necrons: Triggering Reanimations and Reactive Subroutines

Now when your Warriors get a re-roll on their protocols from being near a Canoptek Reanimator, they also get to re-roll the D3 additional wounds from the Nanoscarab reanimation aura. And if you use the Reactive Subroutines Stratagem on Wraiths, it will trigger the unit’s Wraith Form ability.

Orks: Grot Shields Changes

Both of the Ork items here relate to the Grot Shields Stratagem in the Runt Swarm Detachment. The wording on this has been adjusted and cleaned up so after the hit rolls step, your opponent picks one hit, ends the sequence for it, and does a mortal wound to your GRETCHIN unit. They repeat this steps until they’re out of hits or the Gretchin unit is destroyed. This gives the opponent substantially more power and control over the sequencing of attacks and how they’re allocated, and could make a big difference if they have a lot of different weapon types to throw in. There’s also clarification on how this works with [LETHAL HITS] and [SUSTAINED HITS] - they work as you’d expect.

Raven Guard: Shadowmark can’t have other Chapters.

Thus ends our long national nightmare of Guilliman Shadowmark.

Space Marines: Boltstorm Gauntlets lose [Close-Quarters]; selecting doctrines for a unit doesn’t count for the army doctrines.

Two quick clarifications here and Boltstorm Aggressors take another hit.

Space Wolves: Their Detachments can’t have other Chapters.

Similar to tweaks elsewhere. No, they didn’t fix the stupid Wulfen enhancement. No, we don’t know why they didn’t, either.

Ultramarines: Blade of Ultramar can’t have other Chapters.

Just a common sense move.

World Eaters: Defiler and Rhino Tweaks

The Defiler gets rules specifying the model it shoots with the Unleash Wrath ability had to be set up this phase, while the Rhino’s disembark ability specifies it’s a Rapid Disembark. This means that if it arrived from reserves this turn, the disembarking units cannot be within 8” of any enemy units.

Final Thoughts

This is… well, some of these are fine. The Shamblerot fix needed to happen, as did the Deathwatch and chapter-specific updates. But this document causes a few new problems - the notion that terrain listed as 6” away from a table edge is within 6” of that table edge is… certainly something, and has bigger implications we’ll feel later, I’m sure. The rules on leaving the table are also strange, and not having to move maximum distance with surge moves which say “as close as possible” feels wrong and strange.

title: The biggest chase cards in MTG Star Trek
content:
With MTG Star Trek just one week away, and prerelease events kicking off tomorrow, it's not long before fans will be getting their hands on Magic: The Gathering's latest Universes Beyond set. If you're planning to crack packs and want to know what cards constitute a big hit, this guide will break down the highest value pulls you can find in a Play Booster.

That's right, we're only looking at the regular cards and treatments available in Play packs. We're a publication by the people, for the people, so if you want to know what the top cards you can pull in a Collector Booster are (It's almost definitely a Patrick Stewart signed card) then you'll have to look elsewhere.

One last note, I've left off the exact prices for these cards, since at this early stage they're likely to fluctuate wildly and would be instantly outdated. For the stardate reprint cards, which make up much of this list, I've included the price of the cheapest version currently available.

Dr. Beverly Crusher

It's a new type of doubler effect - the life gain triggers doubler. This three mana card is absolutely perfect for lifegain decks, making stuff like Ajani's Pridemade twice as good. However, Bev hangs out at the bottom of this list because she's a lot narrower than she actually appears and likely to drop in price.

The effect doesn't double life gained, nor abilities that check whether life was gained in a turn. It's specifically abilities that trigger when life is gained that this creature cares about.

Captain Jean-Luc Picard

One of the best mono-white commanders I've seen in a while, Captain Picard creates crew members, and when you have enough of them he can tutor spacecraft into play already stationed. There's some neat synergy with the Edge of Eternity card, The Seriema - theoretically if Picard was hit with removal you could tap him and six officers to pull it into play and make him indestructible - neat.

There's another likely reason this card is looking popular currently - Patrick Stewart's sad death last week. Whether you see it as a touching tribute or just a bit ghoulish, the fact remains that a card's connection to a recently deceased celebrity gives it a significant popularity boost - as we last saw with Optimus Prime.

LCARS Shocklands

These powerful lands have come down in value a long way since I first got into Magic, with reprint after reprint making them more accessible. Still, they are always in extremely high demand, and these full art versions are bound to be even more so. Especially since they're textless, so you'll have to be eagle-eyed to stop folks bringing them in untapped and not paying their two life!

Shizo, Death's Storehouse

Cheapest version: $37

If your deck is black and wants to attack it can use Shizo, Death's Storehouse. Since that's an enormous number of decks, this utility land is understandably pricey. This version, reskinned as the Terran Throne Room, shows off a location from Star Trek's own evil Echoverse.

Bruvac, the Gradiloquent

Cheapest version: $45

Spock appears here as probably the best mill creature of all time. Bruvac has only ever been released in limited numbers - in Jumpstart, Ravnica Remastered, and Secret Lair - which has kept the price surprisingly high.

Minamo, School at Water's Edge

Cheapest version: $60

One of the best utility lands Magic has, School at Water's Edge is king of combos, a cEDH staple and also just really, really useful with any Commander that has a tap ability.

Sheoldred, The Apocalypse

Cheapest version: $88

While Benedict Cucumberpatch, The Apocalypse has generated a ton of memes, you're kidding yourself if you think the mirth surrounding this card means it's going to be any less expensive. Hilariously, this is the most valuable MTG Star Trek card you can pull from a regular booster.

If you're going to a prelease tomorrow, come tell us about it over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: The rarest and most expensive Lorcana cards of 2026
content:
What are the rarest, most expensive Lorcana cards? When the characters and films are so beloved by so many, it only makes sense mega-fans are prepared to shell out for a rare Disney card with unique art of their favorite character. This guide covers all the most expensive Disney Lorcana card sales from the most recent sets.

Disney Lorcana may be the newest of the big trading card games, but it has a dedicated fanbase of collectors who will pay a princess' ransom to get their hands on the most coveted cards. Older TCGs may have higher price ceilings - nothing on this list can match the most expensive rare Pokémon cards or expensive Yugioh Cards - but there are some very valuable cards nonetheless! The most expensive Lorcana cards are:

Elsa, Spirit of Winter (Enchanted) - $720

The original Elsa from 2023's The First Chapter set is already a collectible card, but this full art Enchanted variant is in another league. She's a double threat - not just one of the most popular Disney characters of all time, but the first card printed of that character when the game launched. If you've got one, don't let it go…

Hades, Looking for a Deal (Iconic) - $1,067

This is currently the rarest Disney villain card around! Though released alongside the previous Pocahontas in winterwear, and just as rare, this card took a lot longer to rise to the heights. Maybe it's because Hades isn't a princess? Still, this sneaky backstabber spent all of August closing the distance, and finally overtook her just before the month ended, capping out at a high of $1,200 in September.

Cinderella, Unintentional Icon (Iconic) - $1,152

Yes, she's serving. Released in October as part of Hyperia City, Cinderella's highest sale was a cool $1,500. We can understand why she's running behind set-companion Mickey Mouse - Best in Town, thanks to that more dynamic art, but this is no mean performance.

Moana, Curious Explorer (Iconic) - $1,249

Moana was a surprise appearance in Winterspell, a set with a Winter theme, and it seems this explorer's curiosity is so great she didn't have time to dress for the colder weather. Nevertheless, this paper-cut inspired artwork is absolutely adorable, and helps to make this Iconic card so legendary.

Winnie the Pooh, Hunny Wizard (Enchanted) - $1,430

The colors here are making us so hungry. Pooh Bear doesn't have any fancy abilities to show off, but he does have a soothing smile, a fancy cloak, and golden, sugary goodness surrounding him. Those base stats aren't too shabby, either. By the end of August, Winnie the Pooh was getting close to Ariel, after a long time jockeying for position with Moana.

Ariel, Ethereal Voice (Iconic) - $1,482

This ghostly 'Whisper' of Ariel from the Whispers in the Well set not only has a commanding performance, she also commands a high price on the secondary market, which has only crept up since she released - the last sale, in September, hit $1,550

Lilo and Stitch, Fun-Loving Friends (Iconic) - $1,526

There's so much energy and mischief in this Lilo and Stitch card. It looks like the box art for a straight-to-DVD sequel to the classic movie, and we mean that with love: there's no way any actual animation could live up to the sheer action this promises!

Merida - Formidable Archer (Iconic) - $1,828

We all know that Lorcana is a pacifist game, and nobody involved in a challenge is ever hurt - but we have to wonder what Merida does with her arrows to keep her opponents from getting hurt! This is one of the most dynamic princes poses in all of Lorcana. While TCG player's market price is high, recent sales have all been far lower, around $900.

Belle and Beast, Certain as the Sun (Iconic) - $1816

A card as romantic as this was destined to be sought after - Belle and Beast waltzing is a timeless scene from the film that kicked off the Disney Renaissance.  They're also remarkably faithful to their original on-screen appearance as well. After dipping in September, the market valuation is back close to its original $2,000 mark.

Mickey Mouse - Best in Town (Iconic) - $1,861

Of course a new Mickey Mouse would sell like hot cakes - or hot dogs, as this jaunty take on the many-skilled rodent shows. Hyperia City only became available in October so this card is still being opened, but early sales have all clustered around that $2,000 mark. Time will tell if this is his high water mark, or merely the beginning.

Minnie Mouse, Sweetheart Princess (Iconic) - $3,083

When the first Iconic cards were created for Lorcana they were immediately way pricier than anything else on the market, and nearly made it into the all-time top 10, up against extremely rare early promos. Minnie, blowing a kiss in her medieval princess garb, was beginning to slip from her initial high position on the list - but made a recovery in late August as a sheer lack of supply drove up the market price. By October, she was back with a vengeance, with a high sale of $4,200 that's higher than Mickey has ever sold for!

Buzz Lightyear, Jungle Ranger (Iconic) - $3,613

When Wilds Unknown released Buzz Lightyear quickly became the second most valuable card you can open in a booster pack, topping out at $5,700 for a copy. Sales tailed off in June but it's had a few $3,600 sales since then, and it seems that's where it's stabilized.

Mickey Mouse, Brave Little Prince (Iconic) - $3,875

A copy of Mickey hasn't sold since July, so TCG Player's market valuation of $3,875 is very much an extrapolation from the last time the card moved and what would happen if one were to go on sale again. A sudden flurry of movement could result in Mickey being tipped from the top spot, or confirmed in his crown.

If you're a Lorcana collector but not yet a player, you should fix that immediately! It's easy to learn, and we can talk you through which Lorcana starter decks are worth playing.

title: This unofficial Warhammer 40k web client is the kind of training tool I wish GW would make
content:
Despite increasing digital support for miniature wargames, it's rare to find official digital clients that allow you to play virtual versions of games over the internet. Fans tend to fill the gap: War Table supports Warmachine, Eldfall Chronicles, Malifaux, and Guildball, and for just about everything else there are Tabletop Simulator mods. But a new contender has appeared: 'The Old Wargamer', still in development, is a platform that lets you play both Warhammer: The Old World and Warhammer 40,000 in your browser.

The site's mission statement says it's "an unofficial practice tool to learn the games by playing them, where every charge, wound, save and break test is rolled on screen and explained rather than hidden". I've only had a very basic fiddle with each client, but that intent shines through: the site prioritizes surfacing the rules and making explicit what you can do, must do, and can't do at every phase of the game, and it controls the flow of events through phases in a way I've found easy to parse.

Battles are represented in simple 2D that will give older gamers nostalgic flashbacks to 1990s White Dwarf battle reports. Beside them sits a whole panel dedicated to information about the current phase, the unit you may have selected, and the choices you can make.

Creators Ab1t & Dorreah say that they've summarized the rules for the Old World in their own words, with reference to the fan maintained Online Rules Index, while the points and unit options are imported from Old World Builder. Rules for Warhammer 40k factions are taken from Wahapedia's data export.

While the engine doesn't offer a complete simulation of every rule in either game, the framework covers the critical core systems, and the developers have been posting regular updates and bug fixes. The creators specify that they're paying for AI for the website but not how they're using it; presumably as a coding assistant, but perhaps to provide AI opponents for the single-player mode.

You can find details of how to register with the website on Reddit. Whether the web hosting can keep up with increased demand is a real question for this kind of fan project!

Digital wargame clients can be a helpful dojo to practise with an army before you commit to buying it, and allow physically distant players to play friendly matches or participate in virtual tournaments - they really took off during COVID lockdowns. The Old Wargamer's goal of adding much more scaffolding and rules explanation is a smart one. Done right, this could be an excellent training aid, whether you're learning the basics, memorizing your army rules, or really honing your play.

It would be great for Games Workshop to make an official client similar to this, but I can see why it's not a high priority. In this stripped back form it's a tool for people who are already fairly au fait with strategy games even if they're new to Warhammer, and GW doesn't struggle to recruit that audience. Turning it into something more elaborate, a fully fledged Warhammer 40k videogame with the panache to draw in a wider audience and justify an MSRP on Steam is a much bigger and more risky proposition, not least because the game's core systems will need to be reworked every three years. I hope one or the other version happens, but it seems unlikely.

What do you think? What's your preferred way to play Warhammer online when you can't get a game IRL? What tools did you find most useful in helping you learn to play? Share your thoughts in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana Returns – Chaosium’s Definitive Mythos Guide Hits in October
content:
Chaosium is releasing a new fourth edition of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana this October, bringing the definitive guide to Lovecraftian horror back to shelves in full-color hardback format.

First published in 1994 and updated several times since, the book compiles detailed entries on mythos deities, creatures, tomes, and artifacts—from Azathoth to Zylac—tracing their appearances across fiction and pop culture. This new edition features updated text, evocative interior art, and a cover by John Sumrow, along with a fresh essay from author Dan Harms on the question “What is the Cthulhu Mythos?” Timelines of the Necronomicon, a cosmic horror bibliography, and illustrations of Nyarlathotep, Hastur, and Cthulhu himself round out the package.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.
